---
title: "Helmert coding"
---

The [categorical-coding page](coding-categorical-predictors.qmd) showed that a contrast matrix determines the coefficient comparisons. An ordered categorical predictor may support comparisons among successive groups
of levels. Suppose a visual-world experiment presents a preview for 0, 100, 300,
or 600 milliseconds. A processing account may ask whether each longer preview
differs from the average response at the shorter previews.

[**Helmert coding**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=133) constructs those comparisons as orthogonal contrast columns.

The first Helmert contrast
column compares 100 with 0 milliseconds, the second compares 300 milliseconds
with the average of 0 and 100, and the third compares 600 milliseconds with the
average of the three shorter previews.

One common matrix is

| level | $H_1$ | $H_2$ | $H_3$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 ms | $-1$ | $-1$ | $-1$ |
| 100 ms | 1 | $-1$ | $-1$ |
| 300 ms | 0 | 2 | $-1$ |
| 600 ms | 0 | 0 | 3 |

The columns encode distinct comparisons:

1. $H_1$: 100 against 0 milliseconds;
2. $H_2$: 300 milliseconds against the average of 0 and 100;
3. $H_3$: 600 milliseconds against the average of 0, 100, and 300.

The numerical scale of each column matters for coefficient magnitude. For
instance, substituting the first two rows gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{100}-m_0
&=(\beta_0+\beta_1-\beta_2-\beta_3)\\
&\quad-(\beta_0-\beta_1-\beta_2-\beta_3)\\
&=2\beta_1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\beta_1$ is half the difference between 100 and 0 under this unscaled
matrix. The column represents the intended direction, but the coefficient is
scaled by the contrast values.

For the second column,

$$
m_{300}-\frac{m_0+m_{100}}{2}=3\beta_2.
$$

And for the third,

$$
m_{600}-\frac{m_0+m_{100}+m_{300}}{3}=4\beta_3.
$$

These factors of 2, 3, and 4 are why a report should include the matrix rather
than only the contrast name.

## Checking orthogonality

Take the dot product of the first two columns:

$$
(-1)(-1)+(1)(-1)+(0)(2)+(0)(0)=0.
$$

The other column pairs also have dot product zero. This orthogonality means the columns encode nonoverlapping directions in the balanced design matrix.

It does not make the empirical questions theoretically appropriate. The ordering and grouping of levels must come from the linguistic analysis.

Orthogonality is a property of the columns, not evidence for the processing
account. If the scientific hypothesis compares 600 with 0 milliseconds
directly, this Helmert coding makes that hypothesis a combination of several
coefficients. A purpose-built contrast could make the direct comparison easier
to read.

## Setting and inspecting the matrix

```{r}
#| label: inspect-r-helmert-contrasts
#| echo: true
preview_data <- data.frame(
  preview = factor(
    c("0 ms", "100 ms", "300 ms", "600 ms"),
    levels = c("0 ms", "100 ms", "300 ms", "600 ms")
  )
)

contrasts(preview_data$preview) <- contr.helmert(4)
contrasts(preview_data$preview)
```

R's sign convention may be the reverse of a textbook matrix. Reversing an entire column reverses the corresponding coefficient sign but leaves fitted values unchanged.

Contrast terminology also varies across sources. Some sources reserve *Helmert*
for earlier-versus-later comparisons and describe the displayed Helmert sequence
*reverse Helmert*. The name does not settle the interpretation. The printed
matrix does.

## Recovering fitted means

Let

$$
m_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_1H_{1i}+\beta_2H_{2i}+\beta_3H_{3i}.
$$

Substituting each row recovers the four category means. Response-scale predictions remain the most direct way to communicate results, especially in logistic regression where the inverse link is nonlinear.

Suppose the four fitted means are 700, 660, 610, and 600 milliseconds. The encoded
comparisons are then:

$$
660-700=-40,
$$

$$
610-\frac{700+660}{2}=-70,
$$

and

$$
600-\frac{700+660+610}{3}\approx-56.7.
$$

Under the unscaled matrix, the corresponding coefficients are $-20$,
$-70/3$, and $-56.7/4$. These coefficients encode the same comparisons after
accounting for column scaling.

## Distinguishing Helmert from polynomial coding

Helmert coding compares grouped levels. Polynomial coding represents linear,
quadratic, and higher-order trends across equally meaningful ordered positions.
The preview durations here are ordered, but their numerical gaps are not equal.
If the theory predicts change per millisecond, a numeric duration predictor may
represent that claim more directly.

::: {.callout-note title="Read the displayed contrast matrix"}
1. What comparison does $H_2$ encode in the displayed matrix?
2. Why is the comparison involving 300 milliseconds equal to $3\beta_2$ rather than
   $\beta_2$ under the unscaled matrix?
3. What does a zero dot product between two columns establish?
4. Why must a contrast matrix be reported when naming conventions vary?
5. When might numeric preview duration be preferable to four ordered
   categories?
:::
